title: Snake on a Grid
statement:
Build the engine for the classic snake game on a board with height rows and width columns. The snake starts as a single cell at the top-left corner, row 0, column 0.

food lists the cells where food appears, as [row, col], in order: only food[0] is on the board at first, and when it is eaten food[1] appears, and so on. A piece of food never appears on a cell the snake covers at that moment.

  • SnakeGame(width, height, food) sets up the board.
  • move(direction) moves the head one cell: "U" up, "D" down, "L" left or "R" right. It returns the score after the move, which is the number of pieces eaten, or -1 if the game is over.

A move works like this. If the new head cell is off the board, the game ends. If the new head cell holds the current food, the snake eats it and grows by one: its tail stays where it is. Otherwise the tail leaves its cell. Then, if the head lands on a cell still covered by the body, the game ends. Moving into the cell the tail is just leaving is allowed. Once the game has ended, every further move returns -1.

Tests are a list of operations with their arguments; the first creates the game. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: The snake eats at (1, 2) and (0, 1), reaching length 3. The last move turns straight back up into the cell behind its head, which its body still covers.
After three meals the snake fills the whole 2×2 board. It can still circle, because each move steps into the cell its tail is leaving.

hints: Each move adds a cell at the head and, unless the snake ate, removes the cell at the tail. Which data structure is good at adding at one end and removing at the other?
A queue (deque) of body cells handles the movement in O(1). The slow part is asking "does the head hit the body?" if you scan the whole body each time.
Keep a hash set of occupied cells next to the queue. Remove the tail from the set before testing the new head, so stepping into the tail's old cell is allowed, and keep the tail when the snake eats.

explain.intuition:
The snake's body behaves like a queue: each move pushes a new head cell on one end and pops the tail cell off the other. Eating simply skips the pop, which is exactly how the snake grows. A deque (or an array with a moving start index) does both in O(1).

The collision check is what needs care. Scanning the body is O(length) per move, and a long snake makes that slow. A hash set of occupied cells answers "is this cell part of the body?" in O(1), like keeping a Set of selected ids next to an ordered list in a UI. The order of operations matters: pop the tail from both the queue and the set before checking the new head, so following your own tail is legal, and only when the snake is not eating.
steps: Store the body as a queue of cells from tail to head, and a set of encoded cells row · width + col. Start with (0, 0) in both.
On move: if the game is over, return -1. Compute the new head from the current head and the direction; if it is off the board, end the game.
If the new head is the current food, increase the score and the food index, and keep the tail. Otherwise pop the tail from the queue and remove it from the set.
If the set contains the new head, end the game and return -1. Otherwise push the new head into the queue and the set, and return the score.
pitfalls: Checking for a collision before removing the tail. Then a snake following its own tail, as in the second example, dies by mistake.
Removing the tail even when the snake eats. The snake never grows and the collision rules change.
Encoding a cell as row · height + col or similar mismatches. With width columns, use row · width + col, or two different cells share a key.

solutions.title: Array of body cells
solutions.idea: Keep the body in an array and scan it to detect collisions. Simple, but each move costs O(snake length).

solutions.title: Queue plus hash set
solutions.idea: The queue moves the body in O(1); the set answers collision checks in O(1). Remove the tail before checking, unless the snake eats.

followups: Several snakes share the board. What does each move need to check, and in what order should the snakes move?
Show the board after each move in a UI. Which cells change per move, and how would you redraw only those?
